name: Sherlock Holmes
visual_anchor: Silhouette of Sherlock Holmes in a tweed Inverness cape and deerstalker hat peering through a magnifying glass in foggy London.
core_traits: Fictional consulting detective created by Scottish author Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
Renowned for acute logical deductive reasoning and forensic observation skills
Resides at 221B Baker Street in Victorian London with his loyal partner Dr. John Watson
Archenemy is the criminal mastermind Professor James Moriarty

facts_and_myths.claim: Sherlock Holmes explicitly says the exact phrase 'Elementary, my dear Watson' in Arthur Conan Doyle's books.
facts_and_myths.explanation: He says 'Elementary' and 'My dear Watson' separately in several stories, but never spoke that exact combined sentence in any original book.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The famous catchphrase was popularized by later theatrical stage plays and Hollywood films.

facts_and_myths.claim: Arthur Conan Doyle once ended the Holmes stories, then brought Sherlock back after fans complained.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1893 Holmes vanished at the Reichenbach Falls; about 20,000 readers cancelled The Strand Magazine, and Holmes later returned.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Holmes officially returned in 1903 in the story 'The Adventure of the Empty House'.

name: Mickey Mouse
visual_anchor: Mickey Mouse in classic red shorts with two white buttons and yellow shoes, waving happily with white four-fingered gloves.
core_traits: Anthropomorphic cartoon mouse created by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks in 1928
Official mascot and global corporate symbol of The Walt Disney Company
Debuted to global acclaim in the synchronized-sound cartoon 'Steamboat Willie'
Signature features include round black ears, white gloves, and red shorts

facts_and_myths.claim: Walt Disney himself provided the original character voice of Mickey Mouse.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Walt Disney voiced Mickey Mouse continuously in his films and shorts from 1928 until 1947.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mickey was originally going to be named 'Mortimer Mouse' before Walt's wife Lillian suggested 'Mickey'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Steamboat Willie was the first animated cartoon ever produced in human history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Animation had existed for over two decades; Steamboat Willie was landmark because it was the first with synchronized sound.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The early Steamboat Willie version of Mickey entered the public domain on January 1, 2024.

name: Mona Lisa
visual_anchor: Enigmatic portrait of Lisa Gherardini with her subtle smile and sfumato smoky backdrop inside the bulletproof Louvre glass.
core_traits: Masterpiece half-length portrait painting by Italian Renaissance polymath Leonardo da Vinci
Depicts Italian noblewoman Lisa Gherardini, wife of Francesco del Giocondo
Renowned for the subject's elusive, enigmatic subtle smile and sfumato blending technique
Permanently exhibited behind bulletproof glass in the Louvre Museum in Paris

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mona Lisa became the world's most famous painting after it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Before Italian handyman Vincenzo Peruggia stole it, it was admired by critics but not a global sensation; media frenzy made it an icon.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pablo Picasso was briefly questioned by French police as a theft suspect.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mona Lisa is painted on an enormous, room-sized canvas.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The painting is surprisingly modest in size (77 cm × 53 cm) and is painted on a poplar wood panel, not canvas.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many Louvre tourists are surprised by how compact the physical painting actually is.

name: Dr. John Watson
visual_anchor: Victorian British gentleman with a neat mustache and bowler hat holding a leather journal beside a fireplace in a London study.
core_traits: Loyal companion, biographer, and flatmate of Sherlock Holmes
Former British Army doctor who had served in Afghanistan before meeting Holmes
Chronicler who recorded almost all of Holmes's famous investigative cases
Patient, practical foil to Holmes's eccentric genius

facts_and_myths.claim: Dr. Watson tells almost every original Sherlock Holmes story to the reader.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Of the 60 original Holmes stories, Watson narrates 56; Holmes narrates two, and two use an outside narrator.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Watson first meets Holmes in the 1887 novel A Study in Scarlet.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dr. Watson was depicted as bumbling and foolish in Arthur Conan Doyle's original stories.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Doyle wrote Watson as an intelligent, brave, and competent doctor; the bumbling caricature was created by Nigel Bruce in 1940s Hollywood films.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the original stories, Watson is a brave, clever doctor who once played rugby.

name: Professor Moriarty
visual_anchor: Tall, thin Victorian mastermind in dark formal tailcoat with sunken eyes and oscillating head standing menacingly on the cliffs above Reichenbach Falls.
core_traits: Brilliant mathematician and criminal mastermind created by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
Sherlock Holmes's intellectual equal and ultimate nemesis
Called the 'Napoleon of Crime' by Holmes because he secretly plans London's biggest crimes
Disappears with Holmes over the Reichenbach Falls after their famous showdown

facts_and_myths.claim: Professor Moriarty appears as an active character in dozens of Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Moriarty appears in person in only one story ('The Final Problem') and is mentioned in only five others.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Conan Doyle created Moriarty as a final, equally brilliant rival to end the Holmes series.

facts_and_myths.claim: Moriarty wrote a treatise on the binomial theorem that won him a university mathematics professorship.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At age twenty-one, Moriarty published a celebrated mathematical treatise on the binomial theorem that earned him a European reputation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His mathematical genius was combined with inherited criminal tendencies, driving him into organized crime.

name: Frankenstein's Monster
visual_anchor: Towering patchwork creature with pale yellow watery eyes and dark lips standing in a stormy Gothic laboratory full of sparks.
core_traits: Thinking, feeling creature built and brought to life by young scientist Victor Frankenstein
Created by English novelist Mary Shelley in her 1818 masterpiece Frankenstein
Speaks eloquently and reads Milton's Paradise Lost in the original book
Longs for friendship but grows lonely and angry when people reject him for his looks

facts_and_myths.claim: The creature created by Victor Frankenstein is officially named Frankenstein in Mary Shelley's novel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Shelley's original novel, the creature is never given a name and is referred to as 'the creature', 'monster', or 'fiend'; Frankenstein is his creator's surname.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The creature once referred to himself as 'the Adam of your labours' when speaking to Victor.

facts_and_myths.claim: Mary Shelley was only 18 years old when she began writing Frankenstein during a rainy summer in Switzerland.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley started the novel in 1816 at Villa Diodati near Lake Geneva during a ghost story competition with Lord Byron and Percy Shelley.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The summer of 1816 was famously known as the 'Year Without a Summer' due to the volcanic eruption of Mount Tambora.

name: Count Dracula
visual_anchor: Aristocratic Transylvanian nobleman in an elegant black cape with a crimson lining standing at the castle gates under a blood-red full moon.
core_traits: Centuries-old aristocratic vampire from Transylvania created by Irish author Bram Stoker in 1897
Drinks human blood to maintain eternal youth and command nocturnal predators
Possesses shapeshifting powers to transform into a bat, wolf, or mist
Vulnerable to sunlight, garlic, crucifixes, and a wooden stake through the heart

facts_and_myths.claim: In Bram Stoker's novel, direct sunlight instantly incinerates Dracula into dust.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the original novel, sunlight only weakens Dracula and restricts his supernatural powers; the fatal burning effect was invented by the 1922 film Nosferatu.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the book, Dracula can walk around London during broad daylight, though he cannot shapeshift at will.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bram Stoker drew inspiration for Dracula's name from Vlad III, known as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula of Wallachia.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Stoker found the name Dracula in a history book in Whitby Library, meaning 'Son of the Dragon' in Old Romanian.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Stoker originally planned to name his villain 'Count Wampyr' before discovering the name Dracula.

name: Abraham Van Helsing
visual_anchor: Wise Dutch polymath with round spectacles holding a crucifix and wooden stake while examining garlic flowers in a candlelit London parlor.
core_traits: Dutch polymath, doctor, and vampire hunter created by Bram Stoker in Dracula
Mentor and scientific guide to Jonathan Harker, Mina Harker, and Dr. John Seward
Combines cutting-edge medical science, occult folklore, and religious relics to combat vampires
Archetypal monster hunter who tracked Count Dracula back to his Transylvanian castle

facts_and_myths.claim: In Bram Stoker's novel, Van Helsing personally drives a wooden stake through Dracula's heart to kill him.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the climax of the book, Jonathan Harker slits Dracula's throat with a kukri knife while Quincey Morris stabs him in the heart with a Bowie knife.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Van Helsing does stake Dracula's three vampire brides in Castle Dracula, but not the Count himself.

facts_and_myths.claim: Van Helsing holds multiple advanced degrees in medicine, philosophy, and law.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dr. Seward describes him as 'an MD, a PhD, an Litt.D., etc., etc.' and one of the most advanced scientists of his day.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Van Helsing's first name, Abraham, was shared with author Bram Stoker himself.

name: Dr. Henry Jekyll
visual_anchor: Respected Victorian physician in waistcoat holding a glowing bubbling beaker of chemical serum in his dark basement laboratory.
core_traits: Respected, prosperous Victorian London physician and chemist created by Robert Louis Stevenson
Believes that the human soul possesses a dual nature of good and evil
Concocts a chemical potion to separate and isolate his darker impulses
Tragically loses control as his evil alter ego begins emerging spontaneously

facts_and_myths.claim: Dr. Jekyll created the potion with the primary intention of becoming an unstoppable violent monster.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Jekyll intended to separate the two natures so that his virtuous self could do good without temptation, while his darker side could indulge without guilt.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Stevenson wrote the initial draft of the story in three days during a feverish dream.

facts_and_myths.claim: The phrase 'Jekyll and Hyde' became a universal English idiom for someone with two vastly contrasting personalities.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The novella was so instantly popular upon its 1886 publication that 'Jekyll and Hyde' entered dictionaries as a common psychological idiom.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Stage adaptations began appearing in London and New York within months of publication.

name: Mr. Edward Hyde
visual_anchor: Sinister, hunched figure cloaked in oversized Victorian coats stalking through cobblestone London alleyways carrying a heavy cane.
core_traits: Vicious, remorseless alter ego of Dr. Henry Jekyll created by Robert Louis Stevenson
Physically smaller and younger than Jekyll, representing unevolved animalistic malice
Commits horrific acts of violence, including trampling a young girl and murdering Sir Danvers Carew
Gradually overpowers Jekyll's body without requiring the potion to transform

facts_and_myths.claim: Mr. Hyde is described in the novella as a giant, muscular beast like the Incredible Hulk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Stevenson explicitly wrote Hyde as small, pale, and dwarfish, reflecting that Jekyll's evil side was less exercised and developed than his good side.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Later theatrical and comic versions enlarged Hyde into a brutish giant for dramatic visual effect.

facts_and_myths.claim: Anyone who looks at Mr. Hyde in the story feels an inexplicable, haunting sense of deformity and revulsion.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Characters describe him as having an aura of pure deformity and distaste, though none can name a single specific physical defect.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This reaction reflects Stevenson's moral theme that pure evil is instinctively abhorrent to the human soul.

name: The Invisible Man
visual_anchor: Figure wrapped in white medical gauze bandages wearing dark round goggles and a trench coat slowly unwrapping his face to reveal thin air.
core_traits: Brilliant yet megalomaniacal scientist named Griffin created by H. G. Wells in 1897
Discovers how to change the body's refractive index to match air, rendering himself completely invisible
Grows grumpy and reckless while struggling to undo his invisibility experiment
Iconic appearance features a bandaged face, prosthetic nose, and dark sunglasses to conceal his transparency

facts_and_myths.claim: The Invisible Man can pass through solid walls and closed locked doors while invisible.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Griffin is made of ordinary physical matter; he cannot phase through walls, must eat to survive, and can be felt, trapped, and struck.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Food remains visible inside his digestive tract until it is fully assimilated by his body.

facts_and_myths.claim: H. G. Wells first published The Invisible Man in 1897.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The story first ran as a magazine serial in Pearson's Weekly, then became a book later that same year.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wells also wrote The Time Machine, so he is often called a father of science fiction.

name: The Phantom of the Opera
visual_anchor: Mysterious masked figure in evening dress and fedora rowing a wooden gondola across a subterranean lake beneath the Paris Opera House.
core_traits: Deformed musical genius and architectural mastermind created by Gaston Leroux in 1910
Haunts the Palais Garnier opera house from a secret subterranean lair beneath the lake
Wears a mask to conceal his severe facial disfigurement
Secretly coaches young soprano Christine Daae, who calls him her 'Angel of Music'

facts_and_myths.claim: The Phantom of the Opera is a real ghost with magical powers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Erik is a living mortal man with exceptional illusionist, engineering, and ventriloquist skills that fool people into believing he is a ghost.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He helped construct the secret passages in the Palais Garnier while working as an architectural contractor.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gaston Leroux's novel was adapted into the longest-running Broadway show in history by Andrew Lloyd Webber.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Andrew Lloyd Webber's 1986 musical adaptation ran on Broadway for over 35 years and nearly 14,000 performances before closing in 2023.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The famous falling chandelier weighs roughly one ton in the theatrical production.

name: Quasimodo
visual_anchor: Hunched, powerfully built bellringer swinging from the massive bronze bells inside the Gothic stone belfry of Notre-Dame Cathedral.
core_traits: Severely deformed bellringer of Notre-Dame Cathedral created by Victor Hugo in 1831
Raised by the austere Archdeacon Claude Frollo inside the cathedral towers
Deafened by the thunderous ringing of the cathedral's massive church bells
Devotedly loyal to the Romani dancer Esmeralda after she offers him water on the pillory

facts_and_myths.claim: Victor Hugo's original novel has a happy ending just like the Disney film.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hugo's novel ends sadly; the cheerful ending, the songs, and the talking gargoyles were added by Disney in 1996.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Two of Disney's gargoyles, Victor and Hugo, are named after the author Victor Hugo.

facts_and_myths.claim: Victor Hugo wrote The Hunchback of Notre-Dame partly to save the decaying cathedral from demolition.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hugo loved Gothic architecture and wrote the novel to inspire public appreciation, sparking a massive historical restoration led by Viollet-le-Duc.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The French title of Hugo's novel is simply Notre-Dame de Paris, putting the building itself as the true protagonist.

name: Ebenezer Scrooge
visual_anchor: Grumpy elderly Victorian miser in a nightcap and spectacles clutching a ledger in a chilly candlelit counting house on Christmas Eve.
core_traits: Cold-hearted, stingy London counting-house owner created by Charles Dickens in A Christmas Carol (1843)
Famous for his trademark dismissive exclamation 'Bah! Humbug!'
Visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his late business partner Jacob Marley
Transformed into a benevolent philanthropist after journeys with the Spirits of Christmas Past, Present, and Yet to Come

facts_and_myths.claim: Ebenezer Scrooge's famous phrase 'Bah! Humbug!' is spoken by him dozens of times throughout Dickens's book.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Scrooge says the exact phrase 'Bah! Humbug!' only twice in the entire novella, though he uses 'Humbug!' on several occasions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word humbug in 19th-century slang meant deceit, nonsense, or fraudulent sham.

facts_and_myths.claim: Charles Dickens wrote and published A Christmas Carol in just six weeks to help pay off his personal debts.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dickens began writing in October 1843 and completed it in late November; it sold out all 6,000 first-edition copies within six days.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992) cast Michael Caine as Scrooge and Kermit as Bob Cratchit.

name: Oliver Twist
visual_anchor: Frail young orphan boy in tattered Victorian rags holding up an empty wooden bowl before the workhouse master.
core_traits: Impoverished orphan boy created by English novelist Charles Dickens in 1838
Born in a parish workhouse and endured harsh mistreatment by Mr. Bumble
Famously uttered the line 'Please, sir, I want some more' when asking for gruel
Escaped to London and was drawn into a gang of juvenile pickpockets led by Fagin

facts_and_myths.claim: Oliver Twist happily chooses to become a skilled professional pickpocket alongside the Artful Dodger.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Oliver is completely unaware that Fagin's 'game' involves stealing until he witnesses Dodger and Charley Bates rob Mr. Brownlow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When he realizes what they are doing, Oliver runs away in shock and is mistaken for the thief.

facts_and_myths.claim: Charles Dickens wrote Oliver Twist as a fiery protest against the British Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dickens sought to expose the cruelties, starvation, and degradation inflicted on impoverished children in Victorian workhouses.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The novel generated widespread public sympathy and contributed to social welfare reforms in Britain.

name: Dorian Gray
visual_anchor: Handsome youthful aristocratic man in Victorian finery gazing fearfully at a decaying, hideous oil portrait hidden under a purple velvet drape.
core_traits: Youthful, exceptionally handsome gentleman created by Oscar Wilde in his 1890 philosophical novel
Wishes that a painted portrait of himself will age while he remains forever young and flawless
Pursues a life of hedonism, vice, and cruelty influenced by Lord Henry Wotton
His hidden portrait bears every scar, wrinkle, and moral stain of his corrupt sins

facts_and_myths.claim: Dorian Gray paints the enchanted aging portrait with his own hands using dark witchcraft.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The portrait is painted by the gifted artist Basil Hallward, who is infatuated with Dorian's pure youthful beauty; no overt witchcraft is performed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dorian's wish that the painting would age instead of him is granted through an inexplicable supernatural twist of fate.

facts_and_myths.claim: Oscar Wilde's novel was heavily censored by the publisher prior to its first printing due to perceived moral indecency.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lippincott's Monthly Magazine excised roughly 500 words of homoerotic undertones without Wilde's knowledge before publication in 1890.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Passages from the book were later used as evidence against Wilde in his 1895 gross indecency trials.

name: Captain Nemo
visual_anchor: Brooding sea captain in naval tunic standing behind the glowing grand observation window of an advanced submarine gazing into deep ocean trenches.
core_traits: Enigmatic commander of the advanced submarine Nautilus created by French author Jules Verne
Featured in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas (1870) and The Mysterious Island (1874)
Brilliant scientist, engineer, and ocean explorer who rejected all terrestrial civilization
Revealed to be Prince Dakkar, an Indian prince fighting against British colonial imperialism

facts_and_myths.claim: Captain Nemo was originally conceived by Jules Verne as a Polish nobleman seeking revenge against the Russian Empire.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Verne originally wanted Nemo to be Polish, but his publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel insisted on obscuring his origins to avoid offending the Russian book market.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Verne later established Nemo's definitive identity as an Indian prince in The Mysterious Island.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Latin word 'Nemo' chosen by the captain means 'King of the Sea'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Latin, 'Nemo' means 'No one' or 'Nobody', an allusion to Odysseus tricking the Cyclops Polyphemus in Homer's Odyssey.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The historic US Navy nuclear submarine USS Nautilus was named directly in honor of Verne's vessel.

name: Phileas Fogg
visual_anchor: Impeccably dressed Victorian gentleman checking a gold pocket watch while boarding a steam train enveloped in swirling white steam.
core_traits: Methodical, punctual English gentleman created by Jules Verne in Around the World in Eighty Days (1872)
Wagers twenty thousand pounds at the Reform Club that he can circumnavigate the globe in eighty days
Accompanied on his global odyssey by his agile French valet Jean Passepartout
Pursued across oceans and continents by Scotland Yard Detective Fix, who suspects him of bank robbery

facts_and_myths.claim: Phileas Fogg travels around the world primarily in a hot air balloon in Jules Verne's book.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fogg never rides a hot air balloon in Verne's original novel; he travels by steamship, train, elephant, sailing sledge, and schooner.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The famous hot air balloon sequence was invented for the 1956 Hollywood movie starring David Niven.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fogg initially believes he lost his wager by five minutes until discovering he gained a day crossing the International Date Line.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because he traveled east toward the rising sun, he crossed 360 degrees of longitude and experienced 81 sunrises in 80 calendar days.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Passepartout realized the mistake just in time for Fogg to rush into the Reform Club with seconds to spare.

name: Long John Silver
visual_anchor: One-legged pirate quartermaster with a crutch under one arm and a colorful green parrot perched on his shoulder leaning against a ship's galley stove.
core_traits: One-legged pirate quartermaster and ship's cook created by Robert Louis Stevenson in Treasure Island (1883)
Former quartermaster of the dreaded pirate Captain J. Flint
Accompanied by his loud pet parrot named 'Cap'n Flint' that screeches 'Pieces of eight!'
Clever, two-faced pirate who leads a mutiny yet truly cares about young Jim Hawkins

facts_and_myths.claim: Long John Silver lost his leg in a swashbuckling sword duel with Captain Flint.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Stevenson's novel, Silver tells the crew he lost his leg while serving in the Royal Navy under Admiral Hawke during a cannon broadside.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Whether this naval service story was true or a clever fabrication to hide his piratical past is left ambiguous by Stevenson.

facts_and_myths.claim: Stevenson modeled Long John Silver's physical handicap and vibrant personality on his real-life close friend William Ernest Henley.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Henley had a leg amputated due to tuberculosis; Stevenson admired his fierce energy and wrote him: 'It was the sight of your maimed strength that begot John Silver'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Henley is also famous as the author of the beloved Victorian poem Invictus.

name: Jim Hawkins
visual_anchor: Brave young English boy holding a cutlass and an antique parchment treasure map while crouched high in the rigging of the schooner Hispaniola.
core_traits: Young protagonist and narrator of Robert Louis Stevenson's adventure classic Treasure Island (1883)
Discovers a secret treasure map in the sea chest of old buccaneer Billy Bones at the Admiral Benbow Inn
Embarks on the expedition aboard the Hispaniola to Skeleton Island
Overhears Long John Silver's mutiny plot while hiding inside an apple barrel

facts_and_myths.claim: Jim Hawkins discovers Captain Flint's buried treasure buried intact under the marked giant tree.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The treasure cache under the tree had already been dug up years earlier by marooned pirate Ben Gunn, who hid it in his cave.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Silver and his mutineers are furious when they open the pit and find only broken pickaxes and empty earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: Jim Hawkins secretly sails the ship Hispaniola away from the pirates by himself.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Jim cuts the ship loose, outsmarts the pirate Israel Hands, and steers the schooner safely onto the beach at North Inlet.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The whole story began when Stevenson drew a treasure island map to entertain his stepson.

name: Captain Ahab
visual_anchor: Stern, weather-beaten sea captain with an ivory peg leg carved from whale bone staring fiercely into a raging storm from the deck of the Pequod.
core_traits: Vengeful, monomaniacal captain of the whaling ship Pequod created by Herman Melville in Moby-Dick (1851)
Obsessively hunts the giant albino sperm whale that severed his leg at the knee
Walks on a prosthetic peg leg fashioned from the polished jawbone of a sperm whale
Drives his entire crew toward doom in his fanatical quest for cosmic vengeance

facts_and_myths.claim: Captain Ahab is the narrator who speaks the immortal opening line 'Call me Ishmael'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The narrator of Moby-Dick is Ishmael, the sole surviving sailor of the doomed Pequod voyage; Ahab only appears several chapters later.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ahab remains secluded in his cabin for the first part of the voyage before revealing his ivory leg to the crew.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ahab is dragged down to the ocean depths when his own harpoon line snags around his neck.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Melville describes Ahab hurling his final harpoon at Moby Dick, only for the flying hemp line to catch his throat and pull him underwater instantly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ahab's demise symbolizes his utter entrapment by the very obsession he pursued.

name: Moby Dick
visual_anchor: Colossal albino sperm whale with a scarred corrugated brow breaching violently through tempestuous ocean waves, snapping a wooden whaling boat in half.
core_traits: Colossal albino bull sperm whale created by Herman Melville in his 1851 epic novel
Famous among 19th-century whalers for his snow-white hump, crooked jaw, and cunning intelligence
Took Captain Ahab's leg on an earlier voyage, starting Ahab's obsessive chase across the oceans
Rams and sinks the whaling ship Pequod, and the narrator Ishmael is rescued at the end

facts_and_myths.claim: Herman Melville's depiction of a whale sinking a full-sized ship was dismissed as impossible fantasy by critics.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Melville based the climax directly on the real-life 1820 sinking of the Nantucket whaleship Essex by an enraged 85-foot sperm whale.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Melville met the son of the Essex's captain while sailing in the Pacific.

facts_and_myths.claim: Moby Dick was also inspired by a real albino sperm whale named 'Mocha Dick' known to sailors in the 1830s.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mocha Dick was a famous white whale encountered near the island of Mocha in Chile, known for surviving over 100 encounters with whalers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Writer Jeremiah Reynolds described Mocha Dick in an 1839 magazine story that Melville likely read.

name: Don Quixote
aliases: The Knight of the Woeful Countenance
visual_anchor: Gaunt Spanish nobleman in makeshift rusty armor and a barber's brass basin helmet charging on a scrawny horse toward a colossal windmill.
core_traits: Delusional elderly Spanish hidalgo created by Miguel de Cervantes in his 1605 masterpiece
Reads so many chivalric romances that he loses his sanity and decides to become a roaming knight-errant
Rides a scrawny, worn-out nag named Rocinante and dedicates his deeds to his imagined lady Dulcinea del Toboso
Famously mistook giant canvas windmills for vicious monstrous giants and charged them with a lance

facts_and_myths.claim: The English idiom 'tilting at windmills' originates directly from Don Quixote attacking windmills with his lance.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The phrase means attacking imagined enemies or fighting futile, unrealistic battles, derived from Quixote's famous misadventure.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When thrown from his horse by the turning sail, Quixote claimed a magician turned the giants into windmills to rob him of glory.

facts_and_myths.claim: Don Quixote dies in battle defending his beloved lady Dulcinea from rival knights.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Cervantes's second volume, Quixote is defeated in a duel, returns to his village, regains his sanity, denounces chivalry books, and dies peacefully in bed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Cervantes published Part Two in 1615 partly to counter a fraudulent sequel published by an impostor.

name: Sancho Panza
visual_anchor: Plump Spanish peasant in rustic vest riding a loyal grey donkey behind a tall, gaunt armored knight through sun-drenched plains.
core_traits: Shrewd, earthy peasant squire to Don Quixote created by Miguel de Cervantes
Agreed to accompany Quixote after being promised the governorship of an island
Rides his beloved donkey named Dapple and communicates through colorful proverbs
Acts as the realistic, practical voice of reason balancing Quixote's soaring delusions

facts_and_myths.claim: Sancho Panza is granted the actual governorship of an 'island' called Barataria as an aristocratic practical joke.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A local duke and duchess give him the inland village of Barataria to mock him, but Sancho proves to be an unexpectedly wise and just judge.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sancho eventually resigns the governorship willingly, declaring he prefers peaceful poverty over stressful power.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sancho Panza believes without question every fantastical story Don Quixote tells him.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sancho frequently points out the harsh reality to Quixote, pointing out that windmills are windmills and sheep herds are not hostile armies.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite seeing through many delusions, Sancho remains fiercely devoted to Quixote's noble spirit.

name: Robinson Crusoe
visual_anchor: Sun-tanned castaway in rough goatskin clothes and a conical cap carrying a homemade parasol along the shore of a deserted tropical island.
core_traits: Shipwrecked English mariner created by Daniel Defoe in his 1719 foundational adventure novel
Spends twenty-eight solitary years marooned on a remote tropical desert island near Trinidad
Survives through self-reliance, farming, pottery making, and building fortified shelters
Rescues a native fugitive whom he names Friday and teaches English

facts_and_myths.claim: Daniel Defoe based Robinson Crusoe partly on the true adventures of Scottish castaway Alexander Selkirk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Selkirk lived alone for over four years on the uninhabited Pacific island of Mas a Tierra (now Robinson Crusoe Island) before being rescued in 1709.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Unlike Crusoe's 28 years, Selkirk's stay was four years and four months.

facts_and_myths.claim: Robinson Crusoe discovers he is not alone on the island when he finds a mysterious message in a bottle on the beach.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Crusoe is shocked to find a single human footprint in the sand, and it worries him for years.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The solitary footprint scene is one of the most famous suspense moments in English literature.

name: Lemuel Gulliver
visual_anchor: Shipwrecked 18th-century English surgeon tied securely to the beach by thousands of slender threads surrounded by hundreds of tiny six-inch soldiers.
core_traits: English ship surgeon and traveler created by Anglo-Irish satirist Jonathan Swift in Gulliver's Travels (1726)
Visited the miniature kingdom of Lilliput where inhabitants are less than six inches tall
Traveled to Brobdingnag, a land populated by towering giants where he lived in a dollhouse
Encountered the floating scientific island of Laputa and the noble horse race of Houyhnhnms

facts_and_myths.claim: Jonathan Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels originally as an innocent children's fairy tale about tiny people.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Swift wrote the book as a clever satire poking fun at politicians, scientists, and human foolishness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Swift wrote to Alexander Pope that his chief aim was 'to vex the world rather than divert it'.

facts_and_myths.claim: In Lilliput, tiny people argue over which end of a boiled egg to crack first.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Swift used this silly Big-Endian versus Little-Endian quarrel to poke fun at real arguments between groups in Europe.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This satire later inspired computer science terms 'big-endian' and 'little-endian' for memory byte order.

name: D'Artagnan
visual_anchor: Dashing young French swordsman in a wide-brimmed plumed hat and tabard drawing his rapier while standing shoulder to shoulder with three comrades.
core_traits: Hot-headed, brave young Gascon nobleman created by Alexandre Dumas in The Three Musketeers (1844)
Travels to Paris on a yellow pony with dreams of joining King Louis XIII's elite Musketeers of the Guard
Befriends Athos, Porthos, and Aramis after challenging all three to duels on the same afternoon
United by the legendary motto 'All for one, one for all'

facts_and_myths.claim: D'Artagnan is one of the titular 'Three Musketeers' at the start of Alexandre Dumas's famous novel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The three musketeers of the title are Athos, Porthos, and Aramis; D'Artagnan is a cadet in Des Essarts's guards and only becomes a full musketeer later.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: D'Artagnan was based on a real 17th-century French musketeer captain named Charles de Batz-Castelmore d'Artagnan.

facts_and_myths.claim: D'Artagnan and his friends ride to England to recover diamond studs given by Queen Anne of Austria to the Duke of Buckingham.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cardinal Richelieu plots to expose the Queen's secret affection, but D'Artagnan overcomes Richelieu's agents to return the diamonds in time.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dumas wrote the novel in serial installments for the Parisian newspaper Le Siecle.

name: Athos
visual_anchor: Noble, serious French musketeer in a dark velvet doublet and blue musketeer tunic resting his hand on a feathered hat in a Paris courtyard.
core_traits: Eldest, most melancholic, and aristocratic of Alexandre Dumas's Three Musketeers
Secretly Count de la Fere, a disgraced nobleman with a dark, tragic past
Quiet, brave musketeer who rarely speaks but is deeply respected by his friends
Acts as a wise, fatherly mentor and steady moral compass to young D'Artagnan

facts_and_myths.claim: The Three Musketeers share the famous motto 'All for one, one for all!'
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Dumas's novel, Athos, Porthos, Aramis, and D'Artagnan use this motto to promise they will always help each other.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: There are really four heroes, because young D'Artagnan joins the three musketeers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Athos is a jolly, joking musketeer who cares only about feasting and fun.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Athos is serious, quiet, and dignified; Porthos is the flashy one who loves fancy clothes and big meals.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Athos rarely speaks unless necessary and uses hand signals with his silent servant Grimaud.

name: The Count of Monte Cristo
visual_anchor: Pale, elegant gentleman in a tailored dark suit standing on the rocky Mediterranean cliffs of Monte Cristo looking toward the fortress of Chateau d'If.
core_traits: Innocent young French sailor Edmond Dantes wrongfully imprisoned in the grim island fortress Chateau d'If
Created by French literary master Alexandre Dumas in his 1844 serial masterpiece
Educated in prison by Abbe Faria, who reveals the secret location of a vast buried treasure
Escapes by sea, finds a vast hidden treasure, and returns as the mysterious Count

facts_and_myths.claim: Edmond Dantes spent twenty-five years in the dungeons of Chateau d'If before escaping.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dantes was imprisoned for fourteen years, entering the dungeon at age nineteen and escaping at thirty-three.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His real-world inspiration was Francois Picaud, a French shoemaker falsely accused of spying in 1807.

facts_and_myths.claim: Edmond Dantes escapes Chateau d'If by hiding inside a sack the guards toss into the sea.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The guards throw the sack from the island's cliffs; Dantes cuts himself free and swims to safety.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chateau d'If in the Bay of Marseille became a world-famous tourist destination due to Dumas's novel.

name: Sir Lancelot
visual_anchor: Peerless knight in gleaming polished plate armor with a white shield bearing red chevrons charging on horseback through a medieval tourney field.
core_traits: Greatest, most valiant warrior among the Knights of the Round Table in Arthurian romance
Raised by the Lady of the Lake, earning him the title Lancelot du Lac
King Arthur's closest companion and greatest martial champion
Champion jouster who rescues kidnapped Queen Guinevere in Chretien de Troyes's famous poem

facts_and_myths.claim: Sir Lancelot was the knight who successfully completed the Quest for the Holy Grail.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lancelot was not pure-hearted enough; his son Sir Galahad, the purest knight of all, found the Grail instead.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lancelot was allowed only a distant, veiled vision of the Grail that knocked him unconscious for twenty-four days.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lancelot was introduced into Arthurian legend by French poet Chretien de Troyes in the late 12th century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lancelot does not appear in early Welsh tales; Chretien de Troyes made him a star of French knightly poems.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chretien's poem was titled Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart.

name: Queen Guinevere
visual_anchor: Regal medieval queen in emerald velvet royal gown and golden crown seated on an oak throne overlooking the rose gardens of Camelot.
core_traits: Legendary Queen of Camelot and wife of King Arthur in Arthurian romance
Brought the famous Round Table to Camelot as part of her wedding dowry
Known as a graceful, wise queen who hosts the knights' great feasts at Camelot
Rescued from the castle of Meleagant by Sir Lancelot in Chretien de Troyes's poem

facts_and_myths.claim: Guinevere's name comes from the old Welsh name Gwenhwyfar.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Welsh, 'gwen' means white or fair, and it forms the first part of her ancient name.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: One old Welsh text says King Arthur had three queens, all named Gwenhwyfar.

facts_and_myths.claim: Archaeologists have proven that Queen Guinevere was a real historical queen.
facts_and_myths.explanation: No evidence proves Guinevere existed; she is a legendary character from Welsh tales and medieval poems.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Julie Andrews played Guinevere in the 1960 Broadway musical Camelot.

name: Robin Hood
visual_anchor: Heroic outlaw archer clad in Lincoln green tunic and feather-capped hat drawing a yew longbow beneath the massive branches of Sherwood's Major Oak.
core_traits: Legendary heroic outlaw archer of English folklore and medieval balladry
Operates from Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire alongside his band of 'Merry Men'
Famous for his chivalric code of 'robbing from the rich and giving to the poor'
Archenemy of the corrupt Sheriff of Nottingham and usurping Prince John

facts_and_myths.claim: The earliest medieval ballads of Robin Hood explicitly state that he was an aristocratic nobleman named Robin of Locksley.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 14th-century ballads, Robin is a humble yeoman peasant outlaw; the dispossessed Earl of Locksley origin was invented by 16th-century Elizabethan playwrights.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Disney's 1973 film shows Robin Hood as a clever fox and Little John as a bear.

facts_and_myths.claim: Robin Hood is most famous in legend for his skill with a yew longbow.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ballads celebrate his superhuman marksmanship, famously depicting him splitting an opponent's arrow in half during Nottingham archery contests.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sherwood's Major Oak, a legendary Merry Men hideout, is thought to be 800 to 1,000 years old.

name: Maid Marian
visual_anchor: Graceful noblewoman in a deep green hunting cloak drawing a recurve bow beside Robin Hood beneath the dappled canopy of Sherwood Forest.
core_traits: Romantic interest, beloved partner, and equal counterpart of Robin Hood in English folklore
Often depicted as an aristocratic gentlewoman who aids the Merry Men from within the royal court
Celebrated for her independent spirit, sharp intellect, and exceptional skill with a hunting bow
Central figure in May Day festival pageants across England for centuries

facts_and_myths.claim: Maid Marian was present alongside Robin Hood in the earliest 13th-century English ballads.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Marian was originally an independent May Day folk character and was only paired with Robin Hood in the late 15th and early 16th centuries.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In early French pastoral poetry, Marian was a shepherdess courted by a knight.

facts_and_myths.claim: In several classic ballads, Marian disguises herself as a pageboy and fights Robin Hood with swords until recognizing his voice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 'Robin Hood and Maid Marian', both fight fiercely in disguise for over an hour without either besting the other until Robin speaks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This duel established Marian as Robin's martial equal in traditional folklore.

name: Little John
visual_anchor: Gigantic, muscular forest outlaw wielding a heavy seven-foot oak quarterstaff while balanced across a narrow wooden log bridge over a rushing river.
core_traits: Second-in-command of the Merry Men and Robin Hood's most faithful companion
Towering giant standing seven feet tall, playfully dubbed 'Little John' as an ironic joke
Master of the quarterstaff and an archer second in prowess only to Robin himself
First met Robin Hood during a famous quarterstaff brawl on a narrow footbridge

facts_and_myths.claim: Little John was named 'Little' because he was physically the shortest and frailest of the Merry Men.
facts_and_myths.explanation: His birth name was John Little, but Will Stutely humorously christened him 'Little John' because he was an enormous giant over seven feet tall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His christening ceremony involved pouring a jug of brown ale over his head in Sherwood Forest.

facts_and_myths.claim: According to tradition, Little John is buried in the churchyard of Hathersage in Derbyshire, England.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A long grave marked 'Little John' exists at St. Michael's Church in Hathersage; an excavation in 1784 uncovered a massive human femur.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The bone indicated a man standing approximately seven feet, two inches tall.

name: Tarzan
visual_anchor: Muscular, sun-bronzed feral man in loincloth leaping effortlessly between colossal jungle vines over misty equatorial rainforests.
core_traits: Archetypal feral jungle hero created by American author Edgar Rice Burroughs in 1912
Born John Clayton, son of British aristocrats marooned on the Atlantic coast of equatorial Africa
Raised from infancy by Kala and a tribe of great apes in the African jungle
Learns to read English books found in his parents' cabin without ever hearing spoken words

facts_and_myths.claim: In Edgar Rice Burroughs's original novels, Tarzan speaks only in broken, simplistic pigeon English like 'Me Tarzan, you Jane'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the novels, Tarzan is exceptionally articulate, highly educated, and speaks fluent English, French, and several African languages.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The broken English catchphrase was invented for the 1932 film starring Olympic swimmer Johnny Weissmuller.

facts_and_myths.claim: The fictional word 'Tarzan' means 'White Skin' in the language of the great apes created by Burroughs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Burroughs invented a consistent ape language vocabulary; 'tar' means white and 'zan' means skin.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tarzan's ape adoptive mother was named Kala, meaning 'Milk'.

name: Jane Porter
visual_anchor: Refined American young woman in a yellow Victorian dress and pith helmet sketching wildlife inside a canvas explorer tent in the jungle.
core_traits: American heroine of Tarzan of the Apes, created by Edgar Rice Burroughs in 1912
Daughter of eccentric Baltimore professor Archimedes Q. Porter
Stranded on the African coast during a treasure-hunting expedition
Captivated by the mysterious ape-man who repeatedly rescues her from jungle predators

facts_and_myths.claim: In Edgar Rice Burroughs's original novel, Jane Porter was an English noblewoman born in London.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Burroughs's 1912 novel Tarzan of the Apes, Jane is from Baltimore, Maryland, USA; British origins were popularized by later film adaptations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Jane and Tarzan eventually marry and settle in England as Lord and Lady Greystoke before returning to Africa.

facts_and_myths.claim: Jane leaves a letter pinned to Tarzan's cabin door that leads him to pursue her across the Atlantic Ocean.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tarzan learns to write English before speaking it, exchanging written notes with Jane during her stay on the coast.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tarzan travels to Wisconsin in the novel's climax to declare his love for Jane.

name: Mowgli
visual_anchor: Agile Indian boy in loincloth holding a glowing firebrand torch while perched high in a banyan tree beside a black panther.
core_traits: Feral human child raised by wolves in the Seoni jungle of India created by Rudyard Kipling in The Jungle Book (1894)
Named 'Mowgli' meaning 'Little Frog' by Mother Wolf Raksha due to his hairless skin
Educated in the 'Law of the Jungle' by Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther
Hunted relentlessly by the ferocious Bengal tiger Shere Khan

facts_and_myths.claim: Mowgli defeats Shere Khan all alone, with no help from his animal friends.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mowgli and the wolves Akela and Grey Brother drive a herd of buffalo into a ravine to defeat the tiger.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Disney's 1967 film, Mowgli chases Shere Khan away by tying a burning branch to his tail.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rudyard Kipling wrote The Jungle Book while living in a cottage in Vermont, USA.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Although Kipling spent his childhood and early career in British India, he wrote the famous jungle stories in Brattleboro, Vermont.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The stories were originally published in magazines before being collected into book form in 1894.

name: Baloo
visual_anchor: Massive, gentle sloth bear scratching his back against a mossy tree trunk while teaching jungle laws to a small boy.
core_traits: Wise old sloth bear and teacher of the wolf pack cubs created by Rudyard Kipling in The Jungle Book
The only non-wolf allowed to speak at the Seeonee Wolf Pack Council
Serves as Mowgli's strict yet deeply affectionate tutor in the Law and Master Words of the Jungle
Fiercely defended Mowgli against the Bandar-log monkeys and Shere Khan

facts_and_myths.claim: In Rudyard Kipling's original stories, Baloo is a carefree, lazy slacker who sings about the 'Bare Necessities'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Kipling's book, Baloo is a scholarly, strict, and demanding teacher who occasionally clips Mowgli's ears when he forgets his lessons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The carefree jazz-singing personality was created by Walt Disney for the 1967 animated classic.

facts_and_myths.claim: Baloo's name is simply the Hindi word for 'bear' (bhalu).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kipling borrowed several character names directly from common Hindi animal names, including Bagheera (panther) and Hathi (elephant).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Kipling specifically identified Baloo as a brown sloth bear native to central India.

name: Bagheera
visual_anchor: Sleek, muscular black panther with glowing yellow eyes crouching silently along a high mossy tree branch in the Indian moonlight.
core_traits: Sleek black leopard/panther created by Rudyard Kipling in The Jungle Book (1894)
Paid for Mowgli's place in the wolf pack with the gift of a fat bull
Born in captivity in the menagerie of the King of Oodeypore before breaking his cage to return to the wild
Acts as Mowgli's protective, wise guardian and clever jungle guide

facts_and_myths.claim: Bagheera was born in the wild and had never seen human beings before meeting Mowgli.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bagheera was born in an iron cage in a royal zoo; he understood the cruelty of man better than any creature in the jungle.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He bore a bald mark under his chin where the iron collar had rubbed away his fur.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bagheera was feared by every creature in the jungle because he was cunning as Tabaqui and bold as a wild buffalo.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kipling writes that everybody knew Bagheera and nobody dared to cross his path, yet his voice was as soft as wild honey.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Only Mowgli could look directly into Bagheera's fierce eyes without looking away.

name: Shere Khan
visual_anchor: Massive Royal Bengal tiger with amber eyes and razor-sharp fangs pacing aggressively through burning tall grasslands.
core_traits: Fierce, arrogant Royal Bengal tiger who serves as the main antagonist of Rudyard Kipling's The Jungle Book
Born with a crippled leg, earning him the mocking nickname 'Lungri' (The Lame One) from his mother
Sees the man-cub as easy prey and is determined to catch Mowgli
Terrified only of 'The Red Flower', the jungle beasts' name for human fire

facts_and_myths.claim: Shere Khan was named after a legendary Indian emperor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kipling named the tiger after Sher Shah Suri, the 16th-century Afghan warrior king who conquered the Mughal Empire.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: 'Shere' means tiger in Persian/Hindi, while 'Khan' signifies a noble lord or king.

facts_and_myths.claim: Shere Khan survives to the end of Kipling's original stories and becomes Mowgli's trusted friend.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mowgli and the wolf Akela guide a buffalo herd into a ravine, and Shere Khan is defeated for good.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Disney's 1967 film, Shere Khan was voiced by the actor George Sanders.

name: Zhu Bajie
visual_anchor: Anthropomorphic pig warrior in black Buddhist robes carrying a heavy nine-toothed rake across a misty river crossing.
core_traits: Anthropomorphic pig disciple of Tang Sanzang from the classic Chinese epic Journey to the West
Formerly Marshal Tianpeng, commander of Heaven's 84,000 naval soldiers, banished for flirting with the Moon Goddess Chang'e
Wields a legendary nine-toothed iron rake crafted by heavenly divinities
Characterized by hearty gluttony, laziness, and humorous earthly desires

facts_and_myths.claim: Zhu Bajie's Buddhist name 'Bajie' translates literally to 'Eight Precepts' or 'Eight Prohibitions'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tang Sanzang gave him the name Bajie to constantly remind him to abstain from eight Buddhist vices, including lust, greed, and gluttony.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite the name, Bajie frequently succumbs to food and sleep throughout the journey.

facts_and_myths.claim: At the journey's end, Zhu Bajie is granted the ultimate status of a fully enlightened Buddha alongside Sun Wukong.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because his earthly cravings were never completely extinguished, Buddha appointed him 'Cleaner of the Altars' to consume leftover food offerings.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bajie was thoroughly delighted with this duty because he could feast at temples every day.

name: Sha Wujing
visual_anchor: Bearded, red-haired monk in simple robes holding a crescent-bladed monk's spade while standing beside a giant white dragon horse.
core_traits: Third disciple of Buddhist monk Tang Sanzang in the Chinese epic Journey to the West
Formerly the Curtain-Lifting General of the Heavenly Court, exiled for accidentally breaking a crystal goblet
Lived as a fearsome river demon in the Flowing Sands River before joining the pilgrimage
Most obedient, patient, and quiet protector among the three disciples, responsible for guarding the baggage

facts_and_myths.claim: Before his conversion, Sha Wujing wore a necklace strung from nine human skulls around his neck.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The nine skulls belonged to nine previous incarnations of Tang Sanzang whom Sha Wujing had devoured when they tried to cross his river.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The skulls later miraculously formed a raft that carried the pilgrims across the treacherous waters.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sha Wujing frequently quarrels with Sun Wukong and tries to abandon the pilgrimage.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sha Wujing is the most steadfast mediator of the group, constantly resolving arguments between Sun Wukong and Zhu Bajie.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At the end of the journey, he is rewarded with the divine rank of Golden-Bodied Arhat.

name: Tang Sanzang
visual_anchor: Serene Buddhist monk in crimson and gold kasaya vestments wearing a five-pointed crown while riding a noble white steed along a mountain path.
core_traits: Pious Tang Dynasty Buddhist monk and leader of the pilgrimage in Journey to the West
Based on the real historical 7th-century Chinese monk Xuanzang who traveled overland to India
Sent by the Emperor Taizong to fetch sacred Buddhist scriptures (sutras) from the Western Paradise
Demons constantly seek to capture and devour him because eating his flesh grants eternal youth

facts_and_myths.claim: Tang Sanzang fights and slays dozens of demons using martial arts during his journey.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tang Sanzang is a strictly pacifist monk with zero martial ability; he relies entirely on his supernatural disciples to protect him.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: He can control Sun Wukong by reciting the magical 'Tight-Fillet Headache Spell' that tightens Wukong's golden crown.

facts_and_myths.claim: The real historical monk Xuanzang traveled over 10,000 miles across Central Asia and India on a 16-year journey.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Xuanzang left China in 629 AD without imperial permission, studied at the famous Nalanda University, and returned with hundreds of Sanskrit texts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: His travel diary, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, is a priceless historical source for medieval Asian history.

name: Alice (Wonderland)
visual_anchor: Young Victorian blonde girl in a sky-blue pinafore dress tumbling down a surreal vertical rabbit hole lined with floating cupboards, clocks, and bookshelves.
core_traits: Curious seven-year-old English girl created by Lewis Carroll in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865)
Follows a waistcoat-wearing White Rabbit down a rabbit hole into a bizarre nonsense realm
Changes physical size drastically by consuming enchanted cakes labeled 'Eat Me' and liquid from 'Drink Me' bottles
Navigates surreal encounters with the Mad Hatter, the Cheshire Cat, and the Queen of Hearts

facts_and_myths.claim: Lewis Carroll invented the character of Alice to entertain a real ten-year-old girl named Alice Liddell during a boating trip.
facts_and_myths.explanation: On July 4, 1862, Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (Lewis Carroll) rowed a boat on the River Thames and improvised the fairy tale for Alice Liddell and her sisters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alice loved the story so much that she begged Dodgson to write it down for her.

facts_and_myths.claim: Alice escapes the Queen of Hearts by jumping into a magic mirror.
facts_and_myths.explanation: During the trial, Alice grows to giant size, boldly declares the court is 'nothing but a pack of cards', and wakes up on the riverbank beside her sister.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The mirror adventure happens in Carroll's 1871 sequel Through the Looking-Glass.

name: The Mad Hatter
visual_anchor: Eccentric man in an oversized top hat bearing a price card reading 'In this style 10/6' pouring tea from a teapot during an endless outdoor tea party.
core_traits: Eccentric, riddling milliner created by Lewis Carroll in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
Trapped in an eternal tea time alongside the March Hare and the sleepy Dormouse
Famously asks Alice the riddle: 'Why is a raven like a writing-desk?'
Wears a top hat with a paper tag reading 'In this style 10/6' indicating its price

facts_and_myths.claim: The phrase 'mad as a hatter' originated from hatmakers suffering mercury poisoning from felt-curing chemicals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: 18th and 19th-century felt hatters used mercuric nitrate, causing chronic mercury poisoning that led to trembling, mood swings, and hallucinations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lewis Carroll never actually used the words 'Mad Hatter' in the text; he is officially called 'The Hatter'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lewis Carroll provided a canonical solution to the riddle 'Why is a raven like a writing-desk?' inside the novel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Carroll admitted in the book that he had not the slightest idea of what the answer was; decades later he suggested 'Because it can produce a few notes, tho they are very flat'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Author Aldous Huxley proposed another answer: 'Because there is a B in both and an N in neither'.

name: The Cheshire Cat
visual_anchor: Striped magical cat perched on an enchanted forest bough slowly dematerializing until only an enormous mischievous crescent grin remains suspended in air.
core_traits: Mischievous, philosophical grinning feline created by Lewis Carroll in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
Possesses the supernatural ability to appear, disappear, and float at will
Famously vanishes parts of its body gradually, sometimes leaving only its floating smile behind
Guides Alice through Wonderland, noting calmly that 'we're all mad here'

facts_and_myths.claim: The idiom 'grinning like a Cheshire cat' was invented by Lewis Carroll specifically for his book.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The phrase was a common English idiom for over a century before Carroll wrote his book, likely derived from Cheshire cheese molded in the shape of smiling cats.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Carroll grew up in Cheshire, England, and was thoroughly familiar with the local saying.

facts_and_myths.claim: Disney's Cheshire Cat was voiced by Sterling Holloway, the original voice of Winnie the Pooh.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sterling Holloway gave the cat his sleepy, sly voice in 1951 and later voiced Winnie the Pooh.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Disney's film, the cat sings the silly nonsense song ''Twas Brillig'.

name: The Queen of Hearts
visual_anchor: Furious, pompous royal monarch in heart-patterned robes clutching a flamingo mallet while screaming in anger on a surreal croquet field.
core_traits: Fierce, tyrannical monarch of Wonderland created by Lewis Carroll
Quick-tempered ruler famous for shouting 'Off with his head!' at the smallest mistake
Plays croquet using live pink flamingos as mallets and curled-up hedgehogs as balls
Surrounded by a royal court composed of living playing cards

facts_and_myths.claim: The Queen of Hearts's angry orders are actually carried out in Wonderland.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Gryphon tells Alice that nobody is ever really punished; the King quietly pardons everyone behind the Queen's back.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Her furious orders are purely theatrical bluster.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lewis Carroll distinguished the Queen of Hearts from the Red Queen, who appears in Through the Looking-Glass.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Carroll described the Queen of Hearts as uncontrolled blind passion, while the chess-based Red Queen was cold, formal, and pedantic.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern film adaptations, including Disney's, frequently combine both characters into a single queen.

name: The White Rabbit
visual_anchor: Anxious white rabbit in a checked waistcoat pulling a round gold pocket watch on a chain from his pocket while hurrying across an English meadow.
core_traits: Fidgety, time-obsessed rabbit created by Lewis Carroll in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
His frantic appearance muttering 'Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be too late!' lures Alice down the rabbit hole
Wears a tailored waistcoat, carries white kid-gloves, and consults a pocket watch
Serves as the herald and royal court officer for the King and Queen of Hearts

facts_and_myths.claim: The White Rabbit mistakes Alice for his housemaid named Mary Ann and sends her to fetch his gloves.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When Alice reaches his house, she finds another bottle labeled 'Drink Me' that causes her to grow so large she fills the entire room.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The rabbit tries to burn down his own house to get rid of the giant monster inside.

facts_and_myths.claim: The White Rabbit is depicted as brave, aggressive, and hot-tempered in the original novel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lewis Carroll described the White Rabbit as timid, nervous, and obsequious, acting cowardly before the Queen but haughty toward his inferiors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The rabbit represents the anxiety and strict time pressure of Victorian adult society.

name: Peter Pan
aliases: The Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up
visual_anchor: Free-spirited boy clad in autumn leaves and skeleton bark floating weightlessly outside an open nursery window under a starry London night sky.
core_traits: Carefree, mischievous boy created by Scottish playwright J. M. Barrie in 1902 and 1904
Possesses the magical power of flight powered by happy thoughts and fairy dust
Lives in the mythical island of Neverland as the fearless leader of the Lost Boys
Locked in a perpetual swashbuckling rivalry with the pirate Captain Hook

facts_and_myths.claim: J. M. Barrie bequeathed all copyright royalties of Peter Pan to the Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children in London.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1929, Barrie gifted the rights to the children's hospital, providing vital funding for medical care and research for nearly a century.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The UK Parliament passed special perpetual legislation ensuring the hospital continues to receive royalties indefinitely.

facts_and_myths.claim: Peter Pan wears an iconic bright green feathered cap and green tights in J. M. Barrie's original books.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Barrie's play, Peter is dressed in 'autumn leaves and cobwebs'; the iconic all-green feathered cap and tunic were popularized by Disney in 1953.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In early stage productions, Peter Pan was traditionally played by an adult female actress.

name: Wendy Darling
visual_anchor: Gentle Edwardian girl in a pale blue nightgown floating gracefully beside Peter Pan above the illuminated rooftops and Big Ben clock tower of London.
core_traits: Sensible, imaginative eldest daughter of the Darling family created by J. M. Barrie
Flies with Peter Pan to Neverland along with her brothers John and Michael
Acts as a loving, storytelling mother figure to the orphaned Lost Boys
Chooses to return home to London, accepting the reality of growing up

facts_and_myths.claim: J. M. Barrie completely invented the female name 'Wendy' from scratch for his play Peter Pan.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The name was inspired by young Margaret Henley, who called Barrie her 'fwiendy-wendy' because she could not pronounce 'friend'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name Wendy was virtually non-existent before Peter Pan and became a top baby name across Britain and America.

facts_and_myths.claim: Wendy Darling decides to stay in Neverland forever and never grows old.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wendy realizes that growing up is necessary; she returns to London, grows into an adult woman, marries, and has a daughter named Jane.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Peter Pan later returns to take Wendy's daughter Jane to Neverland for spring cleaning.

name: Captain Hook
visual_anchor: Flamboyant pirate captain in an ornate crimson velvet frock coat with an iron hook gleaming on his right wrist standing aboard the Jolly Roger.
core_traits: Swashbuckling pirate captain and arch-nemesis of Peter Pan created by J. M. Barrie
Commander of the pirate galleon Jolly Roger anchored off Neverland
Wears an iron hook in place of the right hand he lost in a duel with Peter Pan
Obsessively terrified of the ticking clock inside the giant crocodile that swallowed his hand

facts_and_myths.claim: Captain Hook was educated at the prestigious English public school Eton College.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Barrie wrote that Hook went to Eton and was obsessed with showing 'good form' at all times.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1927, Barrie gave a famous speech at Eton titled 'Captain Hook at Eton'.

facts_and_myths.claim: In J. M. Barrie's original work, Captain Hook had his hook on his left hand.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Barrie's novel Peter and Wendy, the hook replaces Hook's right hand; left-hand versions appear in later adaptations like Disney's 1953 film.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Barrie's story, Peter Pan tosses Hook's hand to a crocodile, which then follows Hook everywhere.

name: Tinker Bell
visual_anchor: Tiny glowing winged pixie in a leaf-green dress leaving a shimmering trail of golden fairy dust as she hovers inside an antique lantern.
core_traits: Tiny, fiery common fairy created by J. M. Barrie in his 1904 play Peter Pan
Her speech sounds like tinkling bells to human ears
Possesses glowing pixie dust that allows humans to fly when combined with happy thoughts
Fiercely protective of and jealous over Peter Pan

facts_and_myths.claim: In the original stage play, Tinker Bell was represented by a moving dart of light reflected from a mirror offstage.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because theatrical technology could not create a convincing flying miniature person, Barrie used a mirror and electric bulb with a tinkle of bells.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Her voice was produced by a specially crafted set of handbells brought from Switzerland.

facts_and_myths.claim: Tinker Bell was visually modeled directly on Hollywood actress Marilyn Monroe.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Disney animators modeled Tinker Bell on actress Margaret Kerry, who performed live-action reference footage on an oversized soundstage.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Margaret Kerry pantomimed actions like getting stuck in a keyhole using giant studio props.

name: Pinocchio
visual_anchor: Wooden marionette boy with jointed limbs in a yellow cap whose long wooden nose sprouts leafy green twigs and blossoming flowers.
core_traits: Living wooden marionette boy created by Italian author Carlo Collodi in 1883
Carved from a magical piece of talking pine wood by elderly woodcarver Geppetto
His wooden nose grows longer every time he tells a lie
Dreams of transforming from an unruly wooden puppet into a 'real boy'

facts_and_myths.claim: Collodi first planned to end Pinocchio's story much earlier than the finished book.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The story first ran in a children's magazine; Collodi stopped at Chapter 15, but young readers begged for more adventures.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Collodi brought Pinocchio back, and the kind Blue Fairy rescued him to continue the story.

facts_and_myths.claim: Pinocchio's nose grows dozens of times throughout Collodi's original book.
facts_and_myths.explanation: His nose only miraculously lengthens in two specific chapters; Collodi focused more on Pinocchio turning into a donkey on Pleasure Island.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The growing nose became his universal symbol through later theatrical and Disney versions.

name: Geppetto
visual_anchor: Elderly, kindly Italian carpenter in round spectacles and leather apron carving a wooden puppet figure in his warm, wood-shaving-strewn workshop.
core_traits: Impoverished elderly Italian woodcarver created by Carlo Collodi in The Adventures of Pinocchio
Carves the marionette Pinocchio to earn a living traveling the world as a puppeteer
Sells his only winter coat to buy a spelling book for Pinocchio's schooling
Swallowed whole by the Terrible Dogfish while searching the ocean for his missing puppet son

facts_and_myths.claim: In Collodi's original Italian book, Geppetto is swallowed by a giant whale named Monstro.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Collodi's book, the sea creature is 'Il Terribile Pesce-cane' (The Terrible Dogfish), a giant carnivorous shark; Monstro the whale was created by Disney.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Geppetto lived inside the belly of the sea creature for two whole years before Pinocchio found him.

facts_and_myths.claim: Geppetto was nicknamed 'Polendina' by his neighbors because his bright yellow wig looked like cornmeal mush.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Geppetto flew into furious rages whenever anyone called him Polendina, often getting into brawls with his fellow carpenter Master Cherry.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite his fierce temper with neighbors, he loved Pinocchio with absolute tenderness.

name: Jiminy Cricket
visual_anchor: Dapper green cricket in top hat, spats, and waistcoat holding a small opened umbrella while perched on a wooden workbench.
core_traits: Wise insect moral guide created by Carlo Collodi (as the Talking Cricket) and popularized by Disney
Appointed by the Blue Fairy to serve as Pinocchio's official conscience
Sings the immortal Disney anthem 'When You Wish Upon a Star'
Guides Pinocchio away from temptation, indolence, and dangerous companions

facts_and_myths.claim: Jiminy Cricket was voiced by singer Cliff Edwards in Disney's 1940 film.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cliff Edwards, nicknamed 'Ukulele Ike', gave Jiminy his voice and sang 'When You Wish Upon a Star'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: 'When You Wish Upon a Star' won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

facts_and_myths.claim: The character was officially named 'Jiminy Cricket' in Collodi's 1883 Italian novel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Collodi simply called him 'Il Grillo Parlante' (The Talking Cricket); the name Jiminy Cricket was invented by Walt Disney in 1940, derived from a polite 19th-century exclamation for Jesus Christ.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ward Kimball animated Jiminy Cricket for Disney after all his work on Snow White had been cut from the final film.

name: Snow White
visual_anchor: Fair royal princess with skin white as snow, lips red as rose, and hair black as ebony singing gently to forest birds in an idyllic woodland glade.
core_traits: Beloved fairy tale princess recorded by the Brothers Grimm in their 1812 Kinder- und Hausmarchen
Famous for skin white as snow, lips red as a rose, and hair black as ebony
Target of the jealous Evil Queen's wicked tricks after the Magic Mirror names her the fairest
Sheltered deep in the enchanted forest by seven diamond-mining dwarfs

facts_and_myths.claim: In the Brothers Grimm tale, the Prince wakes Snow White with a kiss.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the Grimm version, the Prince's servants stumble while carrying her glass case, and the apple piece pops out.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The famous wake-up kiss was made popular by Disney's 1937 film.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Evil Queen tries to trick Snow White three separate times in the Grimm fairy tale.
facts_and_myths.explanation: She brings tight bodice laces, then an enchanted comb, and finally the famous magic apple.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The dwarfs save Snow White the first two times by removing the laces and the comb.

name: The Evil Queen
visual_anchor: Austere royal queen in a royal purple gown and high cowl gazing into an enchanted ornate golden mirror while holding a shiny red enchanted apple.
core_traits: Vain, sorcerous stepmother of Snow White recorded by the Brothers Grimm in 1812
Consults an omniscient Magic Mirror daily with 'Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?'
Consumes dark potions to transform herself into an ugly peddler crone to deceive Snow White
Crafts the famous enchanted apple, half red and half white, to put Snow White into a deep sleep
distractor_pool: The Wicked Witch of the West

facts_and_myths.claim: The Evil Queen is the very first villain of a full-length Disney animated movie.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was Disney's first full-length animated film, making the Queen its first feature villain.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Actress Lucille La Verne voiced both the proud Queen and her old peddler disguise.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Magic Mirror tells the Queen that Snow White is fairer than her on Snow White's eighteenth birthday.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the original Grimm story, the mirror declares Snow White fairer when she is only seven years old.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Queen's face turns green and yellow with envy when she hears the mirror's verdict.

versus_candidates: The Wicked Witch of the West

name: Cinderella
visual_anchor: Radiant young woman in a sparkling silver-blue ballgown fleeing down palace marble steps leaving a solitary glowing glass slipper on the midnight stairs.
core_traits: Classic folkloric heroine recorded by Charles Perrault (1697) and the Brothers Grimm (1812)
Forced by her cruel stepmother and stepsisters to work as a domestic drudge among chimney ashes
Transformed by a magical Fairy Godmother to attend the royal palace ball in a pumpkin carriage
Flees the palace at the stroke of midnight, leaving behind a delicate glass slipper

facts_and_myths.claim: The glass slippers worn by Cinderella were a mistranslation of French fur slippers ('vair' versus 'verre').
facts_and_myths.explanation: Folklorists have debunked this popular myth; Charles Perrault explicitly wrote 'pantoufles de verre' (glass slippers) deliberately as a miraculous fairy tale element.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In older Chinese versions from the 9th century, the magical slippers were made of spun gold.

facts_and_myths.claim: In the Brothers Grimm version, Cinderella's stepsisters cut off their own toes and heels to force their feet into the slipper.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At their mother's urging, the eldest cuts off her big toe and the younger cuts off her heel; the Prince discovers the trick when white doves sing about blood filling the shoe.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During Cinderella's royal wedding, the doves peck out both stepsisters' eyes as punishment.

name: The Fairy Godmother
visual_anchor: Benevolent celestial matron in a shimmering periwinkle hooded cape waving a sparkling silver wand over a glowing orange pumpkin.
core_traits: Archetypal supernatural guardian introduced into the Cinderella tale by Charles Perrault in 1697
Transforms a garden pumpkin into a gilded royal carriage and mice into dappled horses
Turns Cinderella's cinder-stained rags into a magnificent gown woven of gold and silver
Imposes the strict magical deadline that all enchantments vanish at the stroke of midnight

facts_and_myths.claim: In the Brothers Grimm version of Cinderella, a Fairy Godmother appears with a magic wand to help Cinderella.
facts_and_myths.explanation: There is no Fairy Godmother in Grimm; Cinderella plants a hazel branch on her mother's grave and waters it with tears, and white birds grant her wishes from the tree.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Fairy Godmother, pumpkin coach, and glass slippers were all introduced by French writer Charles Perrault.

facts_and_myths.claim: The magical transformation incantation 'Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo' was created by Disney for the 1950 animated film.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The novelty nonsense song was written in 1948 by Al Hoffman, Mack David, and Jerry Livingston, earning an Academy Award nomination.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The song reached number two on the US Billboard pop music charts in 1949.

name: Sleeping Beauty
visual_anchor: Golden-haired princess in pink royal silk lying asleep on a flower-strewn velvet bed inside a castle tower surrounded by an impenetrable forest of thorns.
core_traits: Cursed royal princess recorded by Charles Perrault (1697) and the Brothers Grimm (1812)
Cursed at her christening by an uninvited evil fairy to prick her finger on a spinning wheel spindle
Saved by a good fairy who softens the curse into a hundred-year sleep
The entire royal castle and all its inhabitants fall asleep until a prince braves the wall of briars

facts_and_myths.claim: In the original Charles Perrault tale, the story ends immediately when the prince kisses Sleeping Beauty and wakes her.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Perrault's tale continues after the wedding, with the prince's ogress mother causing trouble that a clever castle cook outsmarts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Perrault named the princess's two children Dawn and Day.

facts_and_myths.claim: In the Grimm version, the thorn hedge turns into flowers when the hundred years end.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Earlier princes got stuck in the briars, but on the right day the thorns bloomed and let the prince through.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Grimms called their version 'Little Briar Rose', or 'Dornroschen' in German.

name: Maleficent
visual_anchor: Imposing dark sorceress with curved black horns and emerald flame glowing from her golden staff, surrounded by a swirling flock of black ravens.
core_traits: Vengeful dark fairy antagonist created by Charles Perrault and magnificently reimagined in Disney's 1959 Sleeping Beauty
Cursed baby Princess Aurora after being snubbed and excluded from her royal christening
Commands goblin minions, storms of lightning, and an impenetrable forest of black thorns
